query: When was the Western Germanic language spoken from which the small settlement situated on the river Leda opposite Leer derives its name?

pipeline_result.response: The Western Germanic language that the small settlement on the river Leda derives its name from is Afrikaans. Afrikaans evolved from the Dutch vernacular of South Holland (Hollandic dialect) spoken by the mainly Dutch settlers in what is now South Africa, and it developed distinct characteristics starting in the 18th century. The small settlement opposite Leer on the Leda river likely uses Afrikaans as its primary language due to historical influences and linguistic evolution.
retrieved_context: Leda (river): The Leda is a river in north-western Germany in the state of Lower Saxony.  It is a right tributary of the Ems and originates at the confluence of the Sagter Ems and the Soeste (Dreyschloot) near the town of Barßel.  The Leda flows into the Ems near the town of Leer.  On the southern bank of the Leda, in the "Overledingen Land" (Overledingen="country over the Leda"), opposite Leer, lies the small settlement of Kloster Muhde ("Muhde" from the Old Frisian "mutha" meaning "(river) mouth").  The total length of the river is 29 km , of which the lower 1.9 km are navigable for sea-going vessels.

Afrikaans: Afrikaans ( ) is a West Germanic language spoken in South Africa, Namibia and, to a lesser extent, Botswana and Zimbabwe.  It evolved from the Dutch vernacular of South Holland (Hollandic dialect) spoken by the mainly Dutch settlers of what is now South Africa, where it gradually began to develop distinguishing characteristics in the course of the 18th century.  Hence, it is a daughter language of Dutch, and was previously referred to as "Cape Dutch" (a term also used to refer collectively to the early Cape settlers) or "kitchen Dutch" (a derogatory term used to refer to Afrikaans in its earlier days).  However, it is also variously described as a creole or as a partially creolised language.  The term is ultimately derived from Dutch "Afrikaans-Hollands " meaning "African Dutch".  It is the first language of most of the Afrikaners and Coloureds of Southern Africa.

English language: English is a West Germanic language that was first spoken in early medieval England and is now a global "lingua franca".  Named after the Angles, one of the Germanic tribes that migrated to England, it ultimately derives its name from the Anglia (Angeln) peninsula in the Baltic Sea.  It is closely related to the Frisian languages, but its vocabulary has been significantly influenced by other Germanic languages, particularly Norse (a North Germanic language), as well as by Latin and Romance languages, particularly French.
